title: The Solar System and Space Technologies
seo_title: JSS 3 Intermediate Science: The Solar System and Space Technologies Worksheets (NERDC)
standard_code: JSS 3 Intermediate Science: Learning About Our Environment
standard_text: The origin of the solar system; planets, comets and asteroids; galaxies and the universe; space technologies such as satellites and telescopes and their uses. (summary of the Intermediate Science curriculum, JSS 3, theme: Learning About Our Environment)
meta_desc: Free JSS 3 Intermediate Science worksheets (NERDC curriculum, theme: Learning About Our Environment): galaxies and the big bang, the origin of the solar system, the planets, satellites and telescopes and living and working in space. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: The universe began about 13.8 billion years ago and is still expanding.
body_html:
How to think about it

The solar system formed about 4.6 billion years ago from a spinning cloud of gas and dust (the nebular theory): the Sun formed at the centre and planets formed from the disk around it. Comets and asteroids are leftover material. Distances in space are measured in astronomical units and light-years.

Evidence for the big bang includes the red shift of distant galaxies and the cosmic microwave background. Space technology such as satellites for weather, communication and GPS brings many benefits; Nigeria has launched its own satellites, such as NigeriaSat-1 and NigeriaSat-2, to observe the Earth.

Example

Light from a star takes 4 years to reach us. How far away is it?

Distance = 4 light-years

Answer: about 3.8 × 10¹³ km

Example

A galaxy's light is shifted towards red. What does this tell us?

The wavelength is stretched.

Answer: it is moving away from us

Common mistakes

  • Thinking a light-year is a unit of time.
  • Saying all stars end as black holes.
  • Thinking satellites stay up because there is no gravity in space.

faq.q: Why do we see distant galaxies as they were long ago?
faq.a: Their light took millions or billions of years to reach us.
They watch floods and farmland, map the land, and support communication and navigation.

sets.title: The origin of the solar system

items.q: In a star, 4 helium-4 nuclei combine step by step. What nucleus forms?
items.e: Mass number 4 × 4 = 16; atomic number 2 × 4 = 8 (oxygen).

items.q: In a star, 5 helium-4 nuclei combine step by step. What nucleus forms?
items.e: Mass number 4 × 5 = 20; atomic number 2 × 5 = 10 (neon).

items.q: A mineral has 1/32 of its original uranium-235 left (half-life 704 million years). How old is it?
items.e: 1/32 = 5 half-lives; 5 × 704 = 3,520 million years.

items.q: In a massive star, 3 helium-4 nuclei (2 protons each) are built up into one nucleus. Which element is it?
items.e: 3 × 2 = 6 protons → carbon.

items.q: In a star, 9 helium-4 nuclei combine step by step. What nucleus forms?
items.e: Mass number 4 × 9 = 36; atomic number 2 × 9 = 18 (argon).

items.q: Which happened first: the Late Heavy Bombardment of impacts, or the first microbial fossils (stromatolites)?
c: the Late Heavy Bombardment of impacts
They happened at the same time.
items.e: The Late Heavy Bombardment of impacts: about 4 billion years ago; the first microbial fossils (stromatolites): about 3.5 billion years ago.

items.q: In a massive star, 4 helium-4 nuclei (2 protons each) are built up into one nucleus. Which element is it?
items.e: 4 × 2 = 8 protons → oxygen.

items.q: Which happened first: oxygen begins to build up in the air, or the first animals appear?
c: oxygen begins to build up in the air
They happened at the same time.
items.e: Oxygen begins to build up in the air: about 2.4 billion years ago; the first animals appear: about 0.6 billion years ago.

items.q: Which happened first: oxygen begins to build up in the air, or the first microbial fossils (stromatolites)?
c: oxygen begins to build up in the air
They happened at the same time.
items.e: The first microbial fossils (stromatolites): about 3.5 billion years ago; oxygen begins to build up in the air: about 2.4 billion years ago.

items.q: What does this evidence tell us about early Earth: Heavily cratered surfaces on the Moon and Mercury?
c: Simple microbial life existed very early.
Earth had solid crust and probably liquid water very early.
The early solar system had many large impacts.
Oxygen began to build up in the oceans and air.
items.e: Old materials record early events.

items.q: In a massive star, 7 helium-4 nuclei (2 protons each) are built up into one nucleus. Which element is it?
items.e: 7 × 2 = 14 protons → silicon.

items.q: Which happened first: the first animals appear, or the oldest zircon crystals form?
c: They happened at the same time.
items.e: The oldest zircon crystals form: about 4.4 billion years ago; the first animals appear: about 0.6 billion years ago.

items.q: In a massive star, 5 helium-4 nuclei (2 protons each) are built up into one nucleus. Which element is it?
items.e: 5 × 2 = 10 protons → neon.

items.q: In a massive star, 10 helium-4 nuclei (2 protons each) are built up into one nucleus. Which element is it?
items.e: 10 × 2 = 20 protons → calcium.

items.q: Which happened first: the Late Heavy Bombardment of impacts, or the oldest zircon crystals form?
c: the Late Heavy Bombardment of impacts
They happened at the same time.
items.e: The oldest zircon crystals form: about 4.4 billion years ago; the Late Heavy Bombardment of impacts: about 4 billion years ago.

items.q: Which happened first: the Moon forms after a giant impact, or the first animals appear?
c: They happened at the same time.
the Moon forms after a giant impact
items.e: The Moon forms after a giant impact: about 4.5 billion years ago; the first animals appear: about 0.6 billion years ago.

items.q: Which happened first: the first animals appear, or the first microbial fossils (stromatolites)?
c: They happened at the same time.
items.e: The first microbial fossils (stromatolites): about 3.5 billion years ago; the first animals appear: about 0.6 billion years ago.

items.q: In a star, 6 helium-4 nuclei combine step by step. What nucleus forms?
items.e: Mass number 4 × 6 = 24; atomic number 2 × 6 = 12 (magnesium).

items.q: What does this evidence tell us about early Earth: Banded iron formations about 2.5 billion years old?
c: The early solar system had many large impacts.
The solar system, including Earth, formed about 4.56 billion years ago.
The Moon formed from material similar to Earth's, likely after a giant impact.
Oxygen began to build up in the oceans and air.
items.e: Old materials record early events.

items.q: Which happened first: Earth forms, or the Moon forms after a giant impact?
c: They happened at the same time.
the Moon forms after a giant impact
items.e: Earth forms: about 4.56 billion years ago; the Moon forms after a giant impact: about 4.5 billion years ago.

items.q: A person stands on a ship at sea. Which arrow shows the direction that Earth's gravity pulls on the person?
items.e: Gravity pulls toward the centre of Earth, so arrow A (pointing into the globe) is “down” for this person.

items.q: A person stands in Antarctica. Which arrow shows the direction that Earth's gravity pulls on the person?
items.e: Gravity pulls toward the centre of Earth, so arrow C (pointing into the globe) is “down” for this person.

items.q: Which instrument lets you see craters on the Moon from your backyard?
items.e: Telescopes make faraway things look closer.

items.q: What is one cost of space exploration?
c: It is very expensive and uses a lot of fuel.
items.e: People debate how to spend the money.

items.q: Which object in the sky is a star?
items.e: The moon and planets reflect sunlight. The sun makes its own light.

items.q: Why are rockets launched with huge amounts of fuel?
c: They need a lot of thrust to escape Earth's gravity.
Because space is full of air
items.e: Leaving Earth takes a lot of energy.

items.q: What do rovers on Mars do?
c: drive on the surface and study rocks, soil and air
items.e: Rovers are robots controlled from Earth.

items.q: A person stands on a ship at sea. Which arrow shows the direction that Earth's gravity pulls on the person?
items.e: Gravity pulls toward the centre of Earth, so arrow D (pointing into the globe) is “down” for this person.

items.q: Why do astronauts exercise every day on the space station?
c: Without Earth's pull, their muscles and bones get weaker.
items.e: Exercise keeps them healthy.

items.q: A person stands at a place on the right side of Earth. Which arrow shows the direction that Earth's gravity pulls on the person?
items.e: Gravity pulls toward the centre of Earth, so arrow A (pointing into the globe) is “down” for this person.

items.q: What is a satellite?
c: an object that orbits a planet
items.e: The Moon is a natural satellite.

items.q: Why does the sun look much brighter than other stars?
c: It is much closer to Earth than any other star.
Other stars are turned off in the day.
It is the only star that gives off light.
items.e: The sun is about 150 million km away. The next closest star is about 270,000 times farther.

items.q: A star looks very dim from Earth. Which could be true?
c: It must be smaller than a house.
It must not give off light.
It may be very far away.
items.e: Distance can make even a very bright star look dim.

items.q: A person stands at the South Pole. Which arrow shows the direction that Earth's gravity pulls on the person?
items.e: Gravity pulls toward the centre of Earth, so arrow B (pointing into the globe) is “down” for this person.

items.q: Which statement about stars is true?
c: All stars are smaller than Earth.
Stars are closer than the moon.
Many stars are as big as or bigger than the sun.
Stars are holes in the sky.
items.e: Stars look like tiny dots only because they are so far away.

items.q: Why do astronauts wear space suits on a spacewalk?
c: to give air and protect them from extreme temperatures and radiation
items.e: Space has no air to breathe.

items.q: Why can't we see stars during the day?
c: The sun's bright light hides their dimmer light.
Stars move away during the day.
items.e: The stars are still there. Sunlight scattered in the sky outshines them.

items.q: Which is closest to Earth?
items.e: The sun is our closest star.

items.q: How does distance change how bright a light looks?
c: The farther away, the dimmer it looks.
The farther away, the brighter it looks.
Lights look brightest from very far away.
items.e: Light spreads out as it travels, so less reaches your eyes from far away.

items.q: What is the sun?
items.e: The sun is a star, like the stars you see at night.

items.q: Which object has the strongest gravity in our solar system?
items.e: It has the most mass.

items.q: What is a spin-off technology?
c: a product first developed for space that is later used on Earth
a rocket that is used again
a satellite that spins to stay stable
items.e: Examples include better water filters, memory foam and scratch-resistant lenses.

items.q: Which instrument on a satellite measures heat given off by the ground and oceans?
items.e: Warm objects give off infrared radiation, so the sensor can map temperatures.

items.q: What is one reason space exploration is expensive?
c: space has no gravity, so nothing can be built
fuel is free but the paint is costly
rockets, spacecraft and life-support systems must be built and tested to be extremely reliable
satellites can only be launched once a century
items.e: Agencies share costs through international projects such as the space station.

items.q: What is the gravitational field strength on the Earth?
items.e: More precisely 9.8 N/kg.

items.q: What does the size of gravitational attraction between two objects depend on?
c: their masses and the distance between them
items.e: More mass, closer: stronger.

items.q: Is there gravity in space?
c: No, there is none at all.
Yes. Gravity acts everywhere, getting weaker with distance.
items.e: Mass (kg) stays the same; weight (N) depends on gravity.

items.q: Why do outer planets take longer to orbit the Sun?
c: They travel a longer path and move more slowly because the Sun's pull is weaker.
items.e: Distance matters.

items.q: Why do astronauts need spacesuits on a spacewalk?
c: the suits let them breathe the gases in space
the suits stop gravity from acting
space has no air to breathe, almost no pressure, extreme temperatures and strong radiation
items.e: The suit is a small spacecraft with its own air, pressure, cooling and radiation shield.

items.q: Does Earth's gravity reach the Moon?
c: No, it stops at the atmosphere.
Yes. It keeps the Moon in orbit.
items.e: Gravity reaches far into space.

items.q: What is a galaxy?
c: a huge group of billions of stars held together by gravity
items.e: We live in the Milky Way.

items.q: Why is space debris a growing problem?
c: collisions make more pieces, which can damage satellites and the space station
it blocks all sunlight from Earth
items.e: More launches and collisions add to the debris; agencies track larger pieces.

items.q: What is one environmental concern about rocket launches?
c: they release exhaust gases and particles into the atmosphere
they make the Moon move away
items.e: Launches also add to space debris if stages are left in orbit.

items.q: What did the Hubble Space Telescope help astronomers measure?
c: the expansion of the universe and the distances to galaxies
the speed of sound in air
items.e: Hubble observations of distant galaxies refined the age of the universe to about 13.8 billion years.

items.q: How do satellites help us study climate change?
c: they make rain fall over deserts
they remove carbon dioxide from the air
they cool Earth by blocking sunlight
they measure ice cover, sea level, sea-surface temperature and greenhouse gases from orbit
items.e: Remote sensing from orbit gives regular data for the whole planet.

items.q: Which planet takes the shortest time to orbit the Sun?
items.e: It is closest: about 88 days.

items.q: Why do astronauts float on the space station?
c: They and the station are falling around Earth together.
There is no gravity in space at all.
items.e: They are in constant free fall.

items.q: Which quantity stays the same on the Moon as on the Earth: mass or weight?
items.e: Mass (kg) stays the same; weight (N) depends on gravity.

items.q: Why do some Indigenous knowledge keepers and scientists both study the night sky?
c: the sky only changes once a century
stars can be seen only from space
the sky has been used for navigation, calendars and stories for thousands of years
items.e: Many peoples used star patterns to mark seasons for hunting, fishing and planting.

items.q: What is space junk?
c: old satellites and pieces of rockets orbiting Earth
items.e: It can hit working satellites.
